comparisons.peer_summary: AMD faces potential intellectual property infringement claims from third parties that could result in substantial damages, injunctions stopping product sales, or costly licensing and redesign efforts, any of which could have a material adverse effect on the business.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies disclose risks related to intellectual property litigation and licensing, but they focus on different operational angles. Qualcomm specifically worries about 'patent exhaustion' if it is forced to sell chipsets to unlicensed OEMs, which would foreclose its ability to assert patents against those OEMs. AMD discloses a broader risk of third-party IP infringement claims that could result in injunctions stopping product sales or require costly licensing, but it does not mention the specific legal doctrine of patent exhaustion arising from its own sales practices. While both face IP litigation risks, Qualcomm's risk is structural to its licensing model (defensive exhaustion), whereas AMD's is defensive against infringement claims (offensive defense).

sentences.text: If we were required to sell chipsets to OEMs that do not have a license to our patents, our licensing programs could be negatively impacted by patent exhaustion claims raised by such unlicensed OEMs (i.e., claims that our sale of chipsets to such OEMs forecloses us from asserting any patents substantially embodied by the chipsets against such OEMs).

With respect to intellectual property litigation, from time to time, we have been notified of, or third parties may bring or have brought, actions against us and/or against our customers based on allegations that we are infringing the intellectual property rights of others, contributing to or inducing the infringement of the intellectual property rights of others, improperly claiming ownership of intellectual property or otherwise improperly using the intellectual property of others.

These parties may file lawsuits against us or our customers seeking damages (potentially up to and including treble damages) or an injunction against the sale of products that incorporate allegedly infringed intellectual property or against the operation of our business as presently conducted, which could result in our having to stop the sale of some of our products or to increase the costs of selling some of our products or which could damage our reputation.

comparisons.peer_summary: The company's success depends on protecting IP through patents, copyrights, and trademarks; failure to protect IP or limited protection in jurisdictions could harm the business. Licensing obligations from acquisitions or exclusive licenses may limit the ability to assert IP rights, and inability to obtain or renew necessary IP licenses could materially adversely affect operations.
comparisons.comparison: Broadcom acknowledges that licensing its IP, particularly exclusive licenses, may 'limit our ability to assert those IP rights against third parties, including the licensee.' This is conceptually similar to Qualcomm's patent exhaustion concern, as both recognize that licensing activities can constrain future patent assertions. However, Broadcom's risk stems from voluntary contractual obligations (exclusive licenses) limiting enforcement, whereas Qualcomm's risk stems from a legal doctrine (exhaustion) triggered by a mandatory sale to an unlicensed party.

sentences.text: If we were required to sell chipsets to OEMs that do not have a license to our patents, our licensing programs could be negatively impacted by patent exhaustion claims raised by such unlicensed OEMs (i.e., claims that our sale of chipsets to such OEMs forecloses us from asserting any patents substantially embodied by the chipsets against such OEMs).
Licensing of our IP rights, particularly exclusive licenses, may limit our ability to assert those IP rights against third parties, including the licensee of those rights.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intellectual Property Protection and Enforcement Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel faces risks in protecting and enforcing its IP rights due to litigation, varying enforceability, and geopolitical factors, including compulsory licensing. Additionally, licensing practices and industry standard participation may allow competitors to use patents or exhaust rights, impairing IP value.
comparisons.comparison: Intel directly addresses the specific legal mechanism of patent exhaustion that Qualcomm fears. Intel states that under current case law, licenses granted to competitors can 'exhaust our patent rights as to licensed product sales under some circumstances.' This confirms that patent exhaustion is a material risk in the semiconductor IP licensing space. Unlike Qualcomm, which views exhaustion as a negative consequence of a hypothetical requirement to sell to unlicensed parties, Intel acknowledges it as a potential outcome of its existing licensing agreements where competitors hold licenses.

sentences.text: If we were required to sell chipsets to OEMs that do not have a license to our patents, our licensing programs could be negatively impacted by patent exhaustion claims raised by such unlicensed OEMs (i.e., claims that our sale of chipsets to such OEMs forecloses us from asserting any patents substantially embodied by the chipsets against such OEMs).

Some of our competitors have in the past had, and may in the future have, licenses to some of our patents, and under current case law, some of the licenses can exhaust our patent rights as to licensed product sales under some circumstances.

comparisons.peer_topic: Third-Party IP Infringement Claims and Remedies
comparisons.peer_summary: Others may assert that the company's products or processes infringe their IP rights. Such claims could require the company to pay damages, enter license agreements, redesign products, or cease manufacturing/selling in certain jurisdictions, potentially having a material adverse effect.
comparisons.comparison: Micron discloses risks related to third-party IP infringement claims against its products, which could require it to redesign products or cease manufacturing. This is distinct from Qualcomm's patent exhaustion risk. Qualcomm's concern is not about infringing others, but about losing its own right to assert patents due to its own sales practices. Micron's risk is external defense against infringement allegations, while Qualcomm's is internal structural risk to its licensing revenue model.

sentences.text: If we were required to sell chipsets to OEMs that do not have a license to our patents, our licensing programs could be negatively impacted by patent exhaustion claims raised by such unlicensed OEMs (i.e., claims that our sale of chipsets to such OEMs forecloses us from asserting any patents substantially embodied by the chipsets against such OEMs).

As is typical in the semiconductor and other high technology industries, from time to time others have asserted, and may in the future assert, that our products or manufacturing processes infringe upon, misappropriate, misuse, or otherwise violate their intellectual property rights.
• cease manufacturing, having made, selling, offering for sale, importing, marketing, or using products and/or manufacturing processes in certain jurisdictions.

comparisons.peer_topic: Risks from IP protection and litigation costs
comparisons.peer_summary: Protecting IP rights and responding to infringement claims may result in substantial costs, damages, or discontinued product sales, and indemnifying customers may negatively impact operating results.
comparisons.comparison: NVIDIA and Qualcomm both highlight the financial and operational risks associated with IP licensing and litigation, but NVIDIA's disclosure centers on the risks of *infringing* others' IP and the costs of obtaining licenses or facing injunctions if it cannot secure them. Qualcomm, conversely, focuses on the risk that *its own* sales behavior (if mandated to unlicensed OEMs) could exhaust its patent rights, thereby harming its ability to license those same patents in the future. Both involve licensing costs and litigation, but the direction of the risk exposure differs: Qualcomm fears losing its own IP leverage, while NVIDIA fears being forced to pay others or stop sales.

sentences.text: If we were required to sell chipsets to OEMs that do not have a license to our patents, our licensing programs could be negatively impacted by patent exhaustion claims raised by such unlicensed OEMs (i.e., claims that our sale of chipsets to such OEMs forecloses us from asserting any patents substantially embodied by the chipsets against such OEMs).
If infringement claims are made against us or our products are found to infringe a third party's IP, we or one of our indemnitees may have to seek a license to the third party's IP rights.

If we or one of our indemnitees is unable to obtain such a license on acceptable terms or at all, we could be subject to substantial liabilities or have to suspend or discontinue the manufacture and sale of one or more of our products.
